lists.title: Swahili A1 Grammar
lists.description: Foundations: pronouns, the first noun classes, and the -na-/-li-/-ta- tense system.

lists.title: Swahili A2 Grammar
lists.description: The perfect, objects inside the verb, more noun classes, possession, and commands.

lists.title: Swahili B1 Grammar
lists.description: Subjunctive, negation across tenses, relatives, locatives, and habituals.

lists.title: Swahili B2 Grammar
lists.description: The verb-extension system: passive, causative, applicative, stative, reciprocal.

lists.title: Swahili C2 Grammar
lists.description: Mastery: simultaneous -ki-, idiom families, proverbs, and the registers of respect.

points.title: Personal pronouns and ni (to be)
points.function: Introduce yourself and others
points.explanation:
The independent pronouns are mimi (I), wewe (you), yeye (he/she), sisi (we), ninyi (you all), wao (they). 'Ni' is the all-purpose present 'to be' and never changes: Mimi ni mwalimu (I am a teacher), Yeye ni daktari.

Negate it with 'si': Mimi si mwalimu.
points.culture_note: Swahili has no grammatical gender at all — yeye is both 'he' and 'she'. Class membership, not gender, is what organizes the language.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: I am a teacher.
He/she is not a doctor.
You are a student.
I am not a doctor, I am a teacher.
They are farmers.
Juma is a doctor.

points.title: Subject prefixes (ni-, u-, a-…)
points.function: Make the verb agree with who is acting
points.explanation:
Every conjugated verb starts with a subject prefix: ni- (I), u- (you), a- (he/she), tu- (we), m- (you all), wa- (they).

The prefix is obligatory even when the pronoun is said: (Mimi) ninasoma. Learn the six person prefixes first — noun classes add more later.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: I am reading a book.
They study a lot.
He/she is drinking tea.
We are playing football.
Are you working?
You (plural) are cooking food.

points.title: Present tense -na-
points.function: Say what is happening now or generally
points.explanation:
The -na- marker between the subject prefix and the verb stem covers 'am doing' and simple present: ni-na-soma → ninasoma (I am reading / I read), a-na-kula → anakula (she is eating).

Structure is always SUBJECT–TENSE–(object)–STEM.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: She is drinking tea.
We are learning Swahili.
I am reading a book.
The children are playing football.
Father is working.
You (plural) are drinking tea.

points.title: Noun classes: M-/Wa- (people)
points.function: Talk about people, one or many
points.explanation:
Swahili nouns belong to classes marked by prefixes.

Class 1/2 covers people: m-/mw- singular, wa- plural — mtu/watu (person/people), mtoto/watoto (child/children), mwalimu/walimu (teacher/s).

The class controls agreement on verbs and adjectives.
points.culture_note: The class system replaces gender and articles at once; there are around 15 classes, met a few at a time.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: One child, two children.
The teacher is reading.
One person, many people.
The farmers are working in the field.
One student, five students.
The farmer farms the field.

points.title: Noun classes: Ki-/Vi- (things)
points.function: Talk about everyday objects
points.explanation:
Class 7/8 mostly covers things: ki- singular, vi- plural — kitabu/vitabu (book/s), kiti/viti (chair/s), kitu/vitu (thing/s).

Verbs agree with ki-/vi- for these nouns: Kitabu kinapendeza (The book is pleasing).
points.culture_note: Ki- also makes languages and styles: Kiswahili, Kiingereza (English), kifaransa — 'the Swahili way' extended to 'the Swahili language'.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: One book, two books.
The book is on the table.
One chair, three chairs.
One chair is at the table.
Two books are on the table.
One knife, four knives.

points.title: Present negative (si-…-i)
points.function: Say what is not happening
points.explanation:
Negate the present with a negative subject prefix and a final -i: si- (I), hu- (you), ha- (he/she), hatu-, ham-, hawa-.

The -na- disappears and final -a becomes -i: ninasoma → sisomi (I don't read), anakula → hali (she doesn't eat... from -la).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: I don't eat meat.
He doesn't drink coffee.
We don't drink coffee.
drills.hint: to drink + present negative, we (final vowel changes)

drills.translation: Don't you eat meat?
They don't speak English.
The child is not going to school today.

points.title: Past tense -li-
points.function: Say what happened
points.explanation:
Swap -na- for -li- for the simple past: nilisoma (I read), walikuja (they came), tulikula (we ate).

The rest of the verb is unchanged — Swahili tense lives in that one slot.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Yesterday I went to the market.
They cooked food.
We learned Swahili last year.
She wrote a letter yesterday.
I drank tea in the morning.
The children played football yesterday.

points.title: Future tense -ta-
points.function: Say what will happen
points.explanation: The -ta- marker makes the future: nitasoma (I will read), atakuja (she will come), tutasafiri kesho (we will travel tomorrow).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Tomorrow I will go to school.
They will arrive tomorrow.
We will go to the market tomorrow.
I will cook ugali in the evening.
He will write a letter tomorrow.
Will you work tomorrow?

points.title: Question words (nini, nani, wapi)
points.function: Ask what, who, and where
points.explanation:
Question words usually follow the verb: Unasoma nini? (What are you reading?), Nani anakuja? (Who is coming?), Unaenda wapi? (Where are you going?).

Yes/no questions need only rising intonation or an optional opening 'Je,'.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: What are you reading?
Where are you going?
Who is coming?
What is your name?
When will you arrive?
Which book do you like?
Why are you learning Swahili?
drills.hint: why — asking for a reason (two words)

drills.translation: How old are you?
drills.hint: how many — agrees with the noun class (miaka → mi-)

points.title: Adjective agreement
points.function: Describe people and things
points.explanation: Adjectives take the noun's class prefix: mtoto mzuri (a good child) / watoto wazuri; kitabu kizuri / vitabu vizuri. A small set of adjectives (-zuri good, -baya bad, -kubwa big, -dogo small) covers most A1 needs.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: The good children are playing.
The big book is here.
The big house is in town.
The small child is sleeping.
The good books are on the table.
Many people are working.

points.title: Perfect -me-
points.function: Say what has (just) happened
points.explanation:
-me- marks a completed action whose result still matters: nimekula (I have eaten), amefika (she has arrived), wamelala (they are asleep — lit. have lain down).

It often translates English 'have done' or a present state.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: I have eaten.
The guest has arrived.
The children have arrived at school.
We have finished the work.
She has written the letter.
I have already drunk tea.

points.title: Object infixes (-ku-, -m-, -wa-…)
points.function: Say who or what the action is done to
points.explanation: The object goes INSIDE the verb, right before the stem: ni-na-ku-penda → ninakupenda (I love you), a-li-ni-ona → aliniona (she saw me), ni-na-ki-soma → ninakisoma (I am reading it, ki- for a class-7 thing).
points.culture_note: One verb can be a whole sentence: 'Nitakupikia' = I will cook for you.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: I love you.
He saw me yesterday.
I saw you yesterday.
He helps them every day.
They are calling us now.
Mother saw him in the morning.

points.title: Noun classes: Ma- (class 5/6)
points.function: Use the ji-/ma- noun family
points.explanation:
Class 5/6 nouns take (ji)- in the singular and ma- in the plural: jina/majina (name/s), yai/mayai (egg/s), gari/magari (car/s).

Agreement uses li-/ya-: Gari limefika (The car has arrived), Magari yamefika.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: One name, many names.
The car has arrived.
One fruit, many fruits.
One egg, five eggs.
The car is on the road.
The cars are here.

points.title: Noun classes: N- (class 9/10)
points.function: Use the N-class — same shape, singular and plural
points.explanation:
Class 9/10 nouns look identical in singular and plural: nyumba (house/houses), ndizi (banana/s), simu (phone/s).

Agreement tells you the number: Nyumba hii (this house) vs nyumba hizi (these houses); i-/zi- on verbs: Nyumba imejengwa / zimejengwa.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: This house is big.
These two houses are big.
These bananas are sweet.
This letter arrived today.
My house is near the market.
The clothes are very attractive.

points.title: Possessives (-angu, -ako, -ake…)
points.function: Say whose something is
points.explanation: Possessive stems are -angu (my), -ako (your), -ake (his/her), -etu (our), -enu (your pl.), -ao (their), and they take the noun's class agreement: kitabu changu (my book), nyumba yangu (my house), watoto wangu (my children).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: My book is here.
My house is small.
My children are at school.
Where is your book?
His/her house is far away.
His/her car has arrived.

points.title: The -a of association (wa, ya, cha…)
points.function: Link two nouns ('of')
points.explanation: 'Of' agrees with the FIRST noun: mtoto wa mwalimu (the teacher's child), kitabu cha mtoto (the child's book), nyumba ya Juma (Juma's house), majina ya watoto (the children's names).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: The child's book is here.
Juma's house is big.
The teacher's children are here.
The child's name is Juma.
The students' books are on the table.
Mother's clothes are here.

points.title: To have: kuwa na
points.function: Say what people have
points.explanation:
'Have' is 'be with': nina (I have, from ni-na), una, ana, tuna, mna, wana — Nina kitabu (I have a book).

Negative: sina, huna, hana…

Sina pesa (I have no money). Past: nilikuwa na (I had).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: I have a good book.
She has three children.
We have a big house.
Do you have a pen?
They have a farm.
I don't have money, sorry.

points.title: Imperatives and polite requests
points.function: Tell and ask people to do things
points.explanation:
The bare stem commands one person: Soma! (Read!), Njoo! (Come!, irregular).

Plural adds -eni: Someni! The negative command uses usi-/msi- + -e: Usisome! (Don't read!).

Softer requests use the subjunctive: Tafadhali usome (Please read).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Read this book!
Don't make noise!
Come here, please.
Close the door!
Drink a lot of water.
Don't be late to school!

points.title: Subjunctive -e
points.function: Express wants, purposes, and suggestions
points.explanation: Verbs ending in -a switch to -e (no tense marker) after wanting, asking, and purpose: Nataka usome (I want you to read), Alikuja tuzungumze (He came so that we talk), Nifanye nini? (What should I do?).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: I want you to read this book.
Let's go to the market to buy fruit.
I want you to return home early.
It is important that we study every day.
Tell him to come here.
What should I do now?

points.title: Negative past and future
points.function: Deny things in any tense
points.explanation:
Negative past uses -ku-: sikusoma (I didn't read), hawakuja (they didn't come). Negative future keeps -ta-: sitasoma (I won't read), hatakuja (she won't come).

The negative subject prefixes are the same as the present ones.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Yesterday I didn't do work.
She will not come tomorrow.
We didn't go yesterday.
I won't come tomorrow.
They didn't cook food.
Won't you work tomorrow?

points.title: Relative clauses (amba- and -ye-/-o-)
points.function: Say 'who/which' to describe things
points.explanation:
Two strategies: amba- plus the class marker — mtu ambaye anasoma (the person who reads), kitabu ambacho nilinunua (the book which I bought) — or the relative infix inside the verb: mtu anayesoma, kitabu nilichonunua.

Amba- is easier; the infix is more compact.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: The person who is reading is a teacher.
The book that I bought is good.
The house that we bought is big.

drills.sentence: Watu {{answer}} wanafanya kazi hapa ni wazuri.
drills.translation: The people who work here are good.
The person who arrived yesterday is a guest.
drills.hint: to arrive + past with the relative infix (he)

drills.translation: The car that I bought is good.

points.title: Locatives (-ni, kuna/pana/mna)
points.function: Talk about places and what is in them
points.explanation:
Adding -ni turns a noun into a place: nyumba → nyumbani (at home), shule → shuleni (at school).

Existence uses kuna (there is, general), pana (at a definite spot), mna (inside): Shuleni kuna watoto wengi (At school there are many children); negative hakuna.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: The children are at school.
Is there food on the table?
The food is on the table.
Is there water inside the bottle?
My parents are at home.
The books are in the bag.

points.title: Habitual hu-
points.function: Talk about routines and general truths
points.explanation: The hu- marker replaces the subject prefix AND the tense for habitual statements: Yeye husoma kila siku (She reads every day), Watu hunywa chai asubuhi (People drink tea in the morning). Context or a noun supplies the subject.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: She reads every day.
People drink tea in the morning.
She habitually wakes up early every day.
Farmers till the land in the morning.
We go to the market every week.
Children play football in the evening.

points.title: Kuwa in other tenses (alikuwa, atakuwa)
points.function: Say how things were and will be
points.explanation:
'Ni' has no tense, so other tenses borrow the verb kuwa: alikuwa mwalimu (he was a teacher), nitakuwa daktari (I will be a doctor), tumekuwa marafiki (we have become friends).

Same pattern before na: alikuwa na gari (he had a car).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: He was a teacher long ago.
I will be a doctor.
We were at school yesterday.
They will be here tomorrow.
Where were you yesterday?
The weather will be good tomorrow.

points.title: Passive -wa
points.function: Say what was done (without the doer)
points.explanation:
Insert -w- before the final vowel: kusoma → kusomwa (to be read), kupika → kupikwa.

Kitabu kilisomwa (The book was read), Chakula kimepikwa (The food has been cooked). The agent, if said, takes na: kilisomwa na mwalimu.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: The food has been cooked.
The letter was written yesterday.
The door has been closed.
The food was cooked by mother.
This work will be done tomorrow.
The thieves were caught yesterday.

points.title: Causative -isha/-esha
points.function: Say you make something happen
points.explanation:
The causative extension turns 'do' into 'make do': soma (read) → somesha (teach / make read), lala (sleep) → laza (put to bed, irregular), rudi (return) → rudisha (give back).

Mwalimu anawasomesha watoto (The teacher teaches the children).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: The teacher teaches the children.
Please return my book.
Mother feeds the child food.
This news will make people happy.
Juma boiled the water.
Please stop the car.
drills.hint: to stand → causative 'bring to a stop'

points.title: Applicative -ia/-ea
points.function: Do something FOR or TO someone
points.explanation:
The applicative adds a beneficiary: pika (cook) → pikia (cook for) — Ninakupikia chakula (I am cooking food for you); andika → andikia (write to); nunua → nunulia (buy for).

It pairs naturally with an object infix.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Mother is cooking food for the children.
I will write you a letter.
Father bought the children presents.
Please open the door for me.
Mother will bring the guest tea.
My friend wrote me a letter.

points.title: Stative -ika/-eka
points.function: Say something got into a state (or is doable)
points.explanation: The stative describes result-states and possibility without an agent: vunja (break) → vunjika (be/get broken) — Kikombe kimevunjika (The cup is broken); soma → someka (be readable); fanya → fanyika (be doable / happen).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: The cup has broken / is broken.
This work is getting done today.
This door opens easily.
This food has gone bad.
His words are understandable.
The glass broke yesterday.

points.title: Reciprocal -ana
points.function: Say people do things to each other
points.explanation: -ana makes the action mutual: penda → pendana (love each other) — Wanapendana (They love each other); ona → onana (see each other / meet) — Tutaonana kesho (We'll see each other tomorrow); saidia → saidiana (help each other).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: They love each other very much.
See you tomorrow! (we will see each other)
The friends help each other every day.
We met each other at the market yesterday.
The two siblings look very much alike.
These people understand each other well.

points.title: Conditional -ki- (if/when)
points.function: Make real conditions
points.explanation:
-ki- inside the verb means 'if/when (realistic)': Ukisoma, utafaulu (If you study, you will succeed); Mvua ikinyesha, tutabaki nyumbani (If it rains, we'll stay home).

The negative counterpart is -sipo-: Usiposoma, hutafaulu.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: If you study hard, you will succeed.
If it rains, we will stay home.
If you arrive early, we will leave.
If I get money, I will buy a car.
If the children study hard, they will succeed.
If she cooks food, we will eat together.

points.title: Hypothetical -nge- / -ngali-
points.function: Imagine what would (have) happen(ed)
points.explanation:
-nge- is the unreal present/future: Ningekuwa na pesa, ningesafiri (If I had money, I would travel).

-ngali- pushes it into the unreal past: Ungalisoma, ungalifaulu (Had you studied, you would have passed).

Both clauses carry the marker.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: If I had money, I would travel.
Had you studied, you would have passed.
If we woke up early, we would catch the bus.
He would come if he knew.
If you knew, what would you do?
Had it rained, we would have stayed home.

points.title: Narrative -ka-
points.function: Tell a story, action after action
points.explanation:
In narration, -ka- chains events after an initial past: Alienda sokoni, akanunua ndizi, akarudi nyumbani (He went to the market, then bought bananas, then returned home).

It keeps stories flowing without repeating -li-.
points.culture_note: Listen for -ka- in any Swahili story or news report — it is the backbone of narrative style.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: He went to the market and (then) bought bananas.
I got home and then cooked food.
We went to town and saw our friends.
He woke up early and drank tea.
They arrived home and ate food.
I bought a book and began to read.

points.title: Noun class U- (class 11/14: uhuru, ukuta)
points.function: Talk about abstracts and long thin things
points.explanation:
U- nouns cover abstract ideas (uhuru freedom, upendo love, ukweli truth) and long or thin objects (ukuta wall, ufunguo key, uso face). Subject concord is u- (ukuta ulianguka), the -a of association is wa, and adjectives take m-/mw- (ukuta mrefu).

Plurals jump to the N-class (kuta, funguo, nyuso) with its agreements.
points.culture_note: Uhuru (freedom) is one of the great U-class words of East African political history — Uhuru Park in Nairobi, Uhuru Peak on Kilimanjaro.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Independence was gained in 1961.
The wall fell last night.
I have lost the house key.
A mother's love is great.
Tell the truth at all times.
The keys are on the table.
drills.hint: to be (location) with the N-class plural subject

points.title: Noun class Ku- (class 15: kusoma as a noun)
points.function: Use whole actions as subjects
points.explanation: The infinitive doubles as a noun of class 15: Kusoma ni muhimu (reading is important). As a subject it takes ku- agreements (kunafurahisha), its -a of association is kwa (kucheza kwa watoto), and possessives take kw- (kuimba kwake, her singing).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Her singing pleases me.
Swimming needs a lot of practice.
drills.hint: to swim — the action as a noun

drills.translation: Working hard brings success.
Children's playing is important.
Walking every day helps your health.
Living in town has its costs.

points.title: Place classes 16–18 (mahali pa-, ku-, mu-)
points.function: Agree with places, not just point at them
points.explanation:
Swahili has three place classes: pa- for definite spots (mahali pazuri, hapa), ku- for general or distant location (huko, kwetu), and mu- for insides (humo, mna).

Kuna/pana/mna — 'there is' — are these three classes wearing -na.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: This place is suitable for a picnic.
We sat in a nice spot.
Back home there is peace.
In there it is dark.
Our home is a good place.
There at the farm there was a big tree.

points.title: Demonstratives (huyu / hiki / hii… and -le)
points.function: Point at things in any noun class
points.explanation: 'This' is built as h- + the class vowel pattern (huyu mtoto, hiki kitabu, hii nyumba, hili gari, hivi viatu); 'that' swaps to the class concord + -le (yule, kile, ile, lile, vile, wale). Learn them as the class's fingerprint — the demonstrative always tells you the class.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: This child studies well.
Those people come from Kenya.
This book is mine.
This house is very big.
This car is new.
These shoes are yours.
This teacher teaches Swahili.
Those guests come from Tanzania.
This egg is raw.
This room is small.
These books are new.
This pen is mine.

points.title: Comparatives (kuliko, zaidi ya, kama)
points.function: Compare people and things
points.explanation: Swahili compares without changing the adjective: X ni mrefu kuliko Y (X is tall(er) than Y). Zaidi (ya) adds 'more (than)', kama equates (as/like), and the superlative is kuliko wote/zote — 'than all'.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.sentence: Mlima Kilimanjaro ni mrefu {{answer}} Mlima Kenya.
drills.translation: Mount Kilimanjaro is taller than Mount Kenya.
This tea is sweeter than that one.
She likes coffee more than tea.
This student is the cleverest of all.
He is as tall as his father.
Today it is hotter than yesterday.

points.title: Relative of time -po- (nilipofika)
points.function: Say when something happened in one word
points.explanation:
-po- inside the verb builds 'when'-clauses: ni-li-po-fika = when I arrived. The future uses -taka-po- (utakapomaliza, when you finish); kila ninapokuja = every time I come.

One verb does the work of an English clause.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: When I arrived home, the rain began.
When you finish the work, call me.
When he was a child, he lived in Mombasa.
We will leave when the sun rises.
drills.hint: to rise + future when-marker, class-5 subject

drills.translation: Every time we meet, we talk a lot.
The moment he saw danger, he ran.

points.title: Relative of manner -vyo- (unavyojua)
points.function: Say how — 'the way that…'
points.explanation:
-vyo- builds 'the way/how' clauses: kama unavyojua (as you know), jinsi anavyofikiri (how he thinks). The tenseless form suffixes -vyo directly (upendavyo, as you like).

It pairs with jinsi, kama, and kadri.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: As you know, life is not easy.
Do as you like.
I don't understand how he thinks.
Write the letter the way I showed you.
Things didn't go the way we planned.
Explain things as they happened.
drills.hint: to happen + past + how-marker, class-6 subject

points.title: Reported speech (kwamba, kuwa, eti)
points.function: Pass on what someone said
points.explanation:
Kwamba and kuwa introduce reported statements (alisema kwamba atakuja). Reported commands skip them and use the subjunctive (aliniambia nije — she told me to come).

Eti flags hearsay you don't vouch for — often with raised eyebrows.
points.culture_note: Eti carries attitude: repeating a claim with eti signals you find it dubious or cheeky — gossip's favourite word.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: He said that he will return tomorrow.
They told me that the meeting has been postponed.
Apparently the teacher didn't come today!
She told me to come early.
drills.hint: to come + subjunctive, I — reported command

drills.translation: The newspaper says that prices will rise.
He replied that he knows nothing.

points.title: Compound tenses (alikuwa akisoma / amesoma)
points.function: Set one action inside another time
points.explanation:
Kuwa carries the outer tense and the main verb carries aspect: alikuwa akisoma (was reading — ongoing), alikuwa amesoma (had read — completed), atakuwa amemaliza (will have finished).

English needs 'was/had/will have'; Swahili stacks two verbs.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: When I arrived, the children had fallen asleep.
drills.hint: to sleep + perfect, they — inside a past frame

drills.translation: This time yesterday, we were cooking food.
This time tomorrow, we will have arrived.
drills.hint: to be + future — the outer tense carrier

drills.translation: When he came in, mother was reading a letter.
Last year, they were living in Europe.
By June, I will have finished the course.
drills.hint: to finish + perfect, I — inside a future frame

points.title: Reversive -ua / -oa (funga → fungua)
points.function: Undo a verb with one suffix
points.explanation:
The reversive turns an action into its undoing: funga close → fungua open, vaa wear → vua take off, ficha hide → fichua reveal, funika cover → funua uncover, panga arrange → pangua dismantle.

It stacks with the other verb extensions you know.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Please open the door.
When he got home, he took off his shoes.
The journalist revealed a big secret.
After the party, we cleared away the tables.
The child sprang the trap with a stick.
Unwrap your present now!

points.title: Concessives (ingawa, ijapokuwa, licha ya)
points.function: Concede a point and push past it
points.explanation: Ingawa and ijapokuwa open 'although'-clauses; japo does the same solo; licha ya takes a noun ('despite'); hata hivyo pivots a whole sentence ('even so'). Hata + -ki- makes 'even if' (hata akijaribu).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Although it rained, we travelled.
Despite his efforts, he failed.
He went to work although he was ill.
He is poor; even so, he is generous.
Even if he tries hard, he doesn't succeed.
We will continue even though there are obstacles.

points.title: Emphatic ndi- (ndiye, ndipo, ndivyo)
points.function: Say 'that's exactly the one / when / how'
points.explanation:
Ndi- + the class's relative -o builds identity emphasis: ndiye (he's the one), ndipo (that's precisely when/where), ndivyo (that's exactly how), ndicho/ndilo/ndio for the other classes.

It's how Swahili clefts a sentence without changing word order.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: HE is the one who stole the money.

drills.sentence: Hapa {{answer}} tulipokutana kwa mara ya kwanza.
drills.translation: This is exactly where we met for the first time.
That is just how life is.
This book is exactly the one I'm looking for.
THEY are the ones who helped us.
Today is THE day of decision.

points.title: Negative conditional -sipo- (unless)
points.function: Warn about what happens if not
points.explanation: -sipo- packs 'if…not / unless' into the verb: u-sipo-fanya kazi = unless you work. It slots where -ki- and -po- go and pairs naturally with a future consequence.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Unless you work, you won't be paid.
If we don't leave now, we'll be late.
If it doesn't rain, the harvest will be bad.
If he doesn't come tomorrow, we'll start without him.
If you don't learn from mistakes, you will keep repeating them.
If they don't listen, they won't be able to understand.

points.title: Purpose clauses: ili + subjunctive
points.function: Say what something is FOR
points.explanation: Ili introduces purpose and the verb after it goes subjunctive: ninasoma ili nifaulu (I study so that I pass). The subject can switch mid-sentence — ili hewa iingie (so that air comes in).

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: I study hard so that I pass the exam.

drills.sentence: Alinunua simu ili {{answer}} na familia yake.
drills.translation: He bought a phone in order to communicate with his family.
We left early in order to avoid the traffic.

drills.sentence: Kula matunda {{answer}} uwe na afya njema.
drills.translation: Eat fruit so that you have good health.
They planted trees so that the environment be conserved.
drills.hint: to conserve + passive subjunctive, class-6 subject

drills.translation: Open the window so that air comes in.

points.title: Participial -ki- (waliondoka wakiimba)
points.function: Paint two actions in one stroke
points.explanation: Beyond 'if', -ki- marks an action running alongside the main one: waliondoka wakiimba (they left singing), nilimwona akitembea (I saw him walking). English needs '-ing'; Swahili reuses -ki- with the subject repeated on both verbs.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: They left singing.
I saw him walking on the road.
He sat quietly, gazing out of the window.
We crossed the river swimming.
Mother came home carrying the luggage.
Don't eat while walking.

points.title: Kupiga idioms (kupiga simu, picha, hodi)
points.function: Sound native with the 'hit' verb
points.explanation:
Kupiga (to hit) powers dozens of everyday idioms: kupiga simu (make a call), kupiga picha (take a photo), kupiga kelele (make noise), kupiga hodi (announce yourself at a door), kupiga mbio (run), kupiga pasi (iron).

Learn the noun — kupiga does the rest.
points.culture_note: Hodi has no English equivalent: you 'knock' with your voice before entering a home, and the answer is karibu — welcome.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: I will call you tomorrow morning.
The tourists took many photos in the park.
The children are making noise; I can't read.
The visitor called 'hodi' at the door.
drills.hint: the word you 'hit' to announce yourself

drills.translation: He runs every morning on the beach.
drills.hint: running — the 'hit' idiom for a run

drills.translation: These clothes need ironing.

points.title: Methali — proverbs and their grammar
points.function: Deploy proverbs the way elders do
points.explanation: Methali compress grammar you know — habitual hu-, class agreement, parallel clauses — into fixed wisdom: Haraka haraka haina baraka (haste has no blessing); Haba na haba hujaza kibaba (little by little fills the measure). Quoting the right one at the right moment is a mark of eloquence.
points.culture_note: Methali are quoted in courtrooms, parliaments, and daladala buses alike; capping an argument with the right proverb can end it.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: Haste, haste has no blessing.
Little by little fills the measure.
One not taught by their mother is taught by the world.
One finger cannot crush a louse.
Unity is strength, division is weakness.
Slowly is indeed the way to go.

points.title: Respect register (shikamoo, honorific plural)
points.function: Show respect the Swahili way
points.explanation: Elders are greeted with shikamoo and answer marahaba — there is no opting out politely. Respected singulars take plural concords (babu wamefika — grandfather has (respectfully) arrived), requests soften with naomba + subjunctive, and karibu/karibuni welcomes one or many.
points.culture_note: Skipping shikamoo with an elder reads as rudeness, not informality; the honorific plural (wamefika for one person) is everyday respect, not distance.

references.title: Live Lingua — free Swahili courses (FSI/Peace Corps)

drills.translation: The child greeted grandmother: 'Shikamoo!'
Grandmother replied: 'Marahaba, my child.'
Excuse me, may I ask a question.
Guests! Welcome (all of you) to our home.
The elder has (respectfully) just arrived.
drills.hint: to arrive + perfect with the honorific PLURAL concord

drills.translation: May you please give me some water.
drills.hint: to give + subjunctive, you…me — softened request

points.title: Asking about time, manner and kind: lini, vipi, gani, mbona
points.function: Ask when, how, what kind and how come, using the interrogatives that follow the verb or the noun.
points.explanation: Beyond the basic nini, nani and wapi, four more interrogatives cover most everyday questions. Lini asks when and follows the verb: utaondoka lini? Vipi asks how or in what way, and also stands alone as an informal 'how are things?'. Gani asks what kind and is unusual in following a noun rather than a verb, taking no concord at all: chai gani?, umri gani? Mbona asks how come, carrying a note of surprise or complaint, and unlike the others it opens the sentence. None of these move to the front the way English question words do; word order otherwise stays as in a statement.

drills.translation: When will you return from the trip?
drills.hint: the interrogative asking at what point in time

drills.translation: When did the meeting begin?
drills.hint: the interrogative asking at what point in time

drills.translation: How did you get here without a car?
drills.hint: the interrogative asking in what manner

drills.translation: How are things today? How's it going?
drills.hint: the interrogative asking in what manner, used alone as a casual greeting

drills.translation: What kind of tea do you want?
drills.hint: the invariable interrogative placed after a noun

drills.translation: Which book are you reading now?
drills.hint: the invariable interrogative placed after a noun

drills.translation: How come you haven't answered my message?
drills.hint: the sentence-initial interrogative carrying mild reproach

drills.translation: How come you woke up so early?
How old are you?
drills.hint: the invariable interrogative placed after a noun

drills.translation: When shall we see each other?
drills.hint: the interrogative asking at what point in time

points.title: Asking for and giving directions
points.function: Ask where a place is and give directions using the locative copula and the direction words.
points.explanation: A location question pairs the noun with the locative copula and wapi: stesheni iko wapi? The copula carries the noun's class, so it is iko for class 9, liko for class 5, kiko for class 7. Directions themselves rely on a small set: kulia for the right, kushoto for the left, moja kwa moja for straight on, and mbele, nyuma, karibu and mbali for in front, behind, near and far. Each is normally introduced by upande wa, 'on the side of', with the -a of association taking the class 11 concord. Instructions come as bare imperatives — geuka, enda, fuata — and pluralise with -ni for a group.

drills.translation: Where is the station?
Where is the shop?
The hotel is on the right-hand side.
The bank is on the left-hand side.
Go straight on as far as the traffic lights.
drills.hint: the three-word phrase literally meaning one by one

drills.translation: The market is near here.
drills.hint: the word meaning close by, also used to welcome

drills.translation: Turn left after the bridge.
Follow this road to the end.
drills.hint: the imperative meaning go along after

drills.translation: Where is the mosque?

drills.sentence: Uwanja wa ndege uko {{answer}} na mji.
drills.translation: The airport is far from the town.

prerequisites: Asking about time, manner and kind: lini, vipi, gani, mbona

points.title: Numbers 11 to 100, and talking about prices
points.function: Build the numbers above ten with na, and use them to state and ask prices.
points.explanation: Swahili builds the teens transparently: kumi na moja is eleven, kumi na saba seventeen. The tens are ishirini, thelathini, arobaini, hamsini, sitini, sabini, themanini, tisini, and mia is a hundred, so twenty-six is ishirini na sita. Only a few low numerals take a class concord — moja, mbili, tatu, nne, tano, nane — while the Arabic borrowings sita, saba, tisa, kumi and the tens never do. Prices use the currency noun followed by the number: shilingi hamsini na tano. To ask a price, pesa ngapi? or bei gani? both work, and ni ngapi? is the shortest form.

drills.translation: I am seventeen years old.
drills.hint: the linker joining ten to the unit

drills.translation: The class has nineteen students.
drills.hint: the linker joining ten to the unit

drills.translation: The fare is fifty-five shillings.
drills.hint: the ten-multiple that is half of a hundred

drills.translation: The book is sold for twenty-six shillings.
drills.hint: the ten-multiple that is twice ten

drills.translation: I have bought two books.
drills.hint: the numeral two carrying the class 8 concord

drills.translation: There are three people at the door.
drills.hint: the numeral three carrying the class 2 concord

drills.translation: How much is this?
drills.hint: the how-many stem with the class 10 concord

drills.translation: What price is this garment?
drills.hint: the invariable interrogative placed after a noun

drills.translation: I bought four oranges at the market.
drills.hint: the numeral four carrying the class 6 concord

drills.translation: Its price is one hundred shillings.

prerequisites: Asking about time, manner and kind: lini, vipi, gani, mbona

points.title: Negative infinitives with -to-: kutojua, kutokuwa
points.function: Negate an infinitive by inserting -to- between ku- and the stem.
points.explanation: Swahili negates a finite verb with a subject prefix, but an infinitive has none, so a different device is used: the infix -to- placed straight after ku-. Kujua is 'to know', kutojua 'not to know'; kuwa is 'to be', kutokuwa 'not to be'. The resulting form behaves exactly like any other infinitive and can follow a preposition, a verb, or stand as a class 15 noun. It is common in formal registers and in writing — kutokuwepo, 'absence', is built the same way. Note that the negative subjunctive uses -si- instead, so usiende means 'don't go'.

drills.translation: He was blamed for not telling the truth.
drills.hint: the negative infinitive of the verb meaning to say

drills.translation: Not knowing is not your fault.
drills.hint: the negative infinitive of the verb meaning to know

drills.translation: He succeeded by not giving up.
drills.hint: the negative infinitive of the phrase meaning to lose hope

drills.translation: That news seemed unbelievable.
drills.hint: the negative infinitive of the verb meaning to be credible

drills.translation: Not being careful can cause an accident.
drills.hint: the negative infinitive of the verb meaning to be

drills.translation: His absence saddened everyone.
drills.hint: the negative infinitive meaning failing to be present

drills.translation: Don't go alone at night.
drills.hint: the second person negative subjunctive of the verb meaning to go

drills.translation: He ran so that he would not be late.
drills.hint: the class 1 negative subjunctive of the verb meaning to be late

drills.translation: I regret not arriving early.
drills.hint: the negative infinitive of the verb meaning to arrive

drills.translation: Not paying on time caused problems.
drills.hint: the negative infinitive of the verb meaning to pay

points.title: The -enye construction: possessing a quality
points.function: Describe a noun by what it has, using the class-agreeing -enye.
points.explanation: Where English uses 'with' or a relative clause, Swahili often uses -enye, meaning 'having' or 'possessing'. It takes the concord of the noun it describes and is followed directly by a noun: mtu mwenye pesa is 'a person with money', watu wenye ulemavu 'people with disabilities', nyumba yenye bustani 'a house with a garden'. The concords follow the ordinary pattern — mwenye for class 1, wenye for class 2, chenye for class 7, lenye for class 5, yenye for class 9. Its negative counterpart is -sio na, or the fuller relative construction. Note that mwenyeji, 'host', is built from the same stem.

drills.translation: People with disabilities deserve equal opportunities.
drills.hint: the class 2 form of the having-stem

drills.translation: He is a person with a good heart.
drills.hint: the class 1 form of the having-stem

drills.translation: We are looking for a house with a garden.
drills.hint: the class 9 form of the having-stem

drills.translation: She bought clothes with bright colours.
drills.hint: the class 10 form of the having-stem

drills.translation: It is an area with great fertility.
drills.hint: the class 5 form of the having-stem

drills.translation: We stayed in a room with large windows.
drills.hint: the class 7 form of the having-stem

drills.translation: He is a person without any worry.
drills.hint: the class 1 negative relative form, used before 'na'

drills.translation: A room without windows is dark.
drills.hint: the class 7 negative relative form, used before 'na'

drills.translation: It is a town with a long history.
drills.hint: the class 3 form of the having-stem

drills.translation: Students with diligence usually pass.
drills.hint: the class 2 form of the having-stem

points.title: Greetings with habari and the possessive concord
points.function: Greet somebody by asking after them with habari, choosing the right possessive or -a form.
points.explanation: The everyday greeting is built on habari, literally 'news'. Habari is a class 9 noun, so anything agreeing with it takes the class 9 concord y-. Addressing one person gives habari yako; addressing several gives habari yenu. To ask after a thing or a period rather than a person, the -a of association is used instead: habari ya asubuhi for the morning, habari ya kazi for work, habari ya Nairobi for a place. The expected reply is mzuri or nzuri, usually strengthened to mzuri sana. Habari alone, with nothing after it, is a safe general greeting.

drills.translation: How are you, Juma?
drills.hint: the class 9 possessive addressed to one person

drills.translation: Respectful greetings, grandmother, how are you?
drills.hint: the class 9 possessive addressed to one person

drills.translation: How are you all?
drills.hint: the class 9 possessive addressed to several people

drills.translation: Welcome, how are you, guests?
drills.hint: the class 9 possessive addressed to several people

drills.translation: Good morning.
drills.hint: the class 9 associative linker before a noun

drills.translation: How is your new job?
drills.hint: the class 9 associative linker before a noun

drills.translation: Good evening. Very well.
drills.hint: the standard one-word reply meaning fine

drills.translation: Good afternoon. Very well.
drills.hint: the noun for the middle of the day

points.title: Introducing yourself: naitwa and jina langu
points.function: Give your own name and ask somebody else's, using either the verb or the noun construction.
points.explanation: There are two routine ways to give a name. The verb route uses -itwa, the passive of -ita 'to call', so naitwa means literally 'I am called'. Because the subject prefix carries the person, no pronoun is needed: naitwa Amina. The same verb asks the question, with nani 'who' after it: unaitwa nani? The noun route uses jina, a class 5 noun, so its possessive takes the class 5 concord l-: jina langu ni Amina. The plural majina takes class 6 y-: majina yangu. Answering an introduction, nimefurahia kukujua expresses pleasure at meeting.

drills.translation: My name is Fatuma Ali.
drills.hint: first person present of the verb meaning be called

drills.translation: I am called Musa; I am a teacher.
drills.hint: first person present of the verb meaning be called

drills.translation: What are you called?
drills.hint: second person present of the verb meaning be called

drills.translation: What is your friend called?
drills.hint: class 1 present of the verb meaning be called

drills.translation: My name is Rehema.
drills.hint: the class 5 possessive meaning belonging to me

drills.translation: What is your name?
drills.hint: the class 5 possessive meaning belonging to you

drills.translation: I am pleased to know you.
drills.hint: the infinitive carrying a second person object infix, meaning to be acquainted with you

drills.translation: My names are Njoroge.
drills.hint: the class 6 plural of the word for name

prerequisites: Greetings with habari and the possessive concord

points.title: Telling the time: the Swahili saa system
points.function: Read and say clock times in Swahili, allowing for the six-hour offset from the international clock.
points.explanation: Swahili counts the hours from dawn rather than from midnight, so the Swahili hour runs six hours behind the clock on the wall. Seven o'clock in the morning is saa moja asubuhi, literally 'hour one of the morning', because it is the first hour after sunrise. One o'clock in the afternoon is saa saba, the seventh hour. The rule is simple: subtract six, or add six, to convert. The period word follows the number — asubuhi for the morning, mchana for the afternoon, jioni for the evening, usiku for the night. To ask the time, saa ngapi? uses the class 9 concord on -ngapi.

drills.translation: What time is it now?
drills.hint: the how-many stem carrying the class 9 concord

drills.translation: At what time will we leave?
drills.hint: the how-many stem carrying the class 9 concord

drills.sentence: Ninaamka saa {{answer}} asubuhi, yaani saa saba za usiku wa manane zikiisha.
drills.translation: I get up at seven in the morning.
drills.hint: the numeral for a single unit, giving seven o'clock

drills.translation: The class begins at nine in the morning.
drills.hint: the numeral between two and four, giving nine o'clock

drills.translation: We eat lunch at one o'clock.
drills.hint: the numeral one less than eight, giving one in the afternoon

drills.translation: The shop closes at four in the afternoon.
drills.hint: the numeral for a full set of fingers, giving four o'clock

drills.sentence: Saa sita {{answer}} ni saa kumi na mbili za mchana kwa saa za kimataifa.
drills.translation: Saa sita in the daytime is twelve noon by the international clock.
drills.hint: the period word for the middle of the day

drills.translation: The plane will leave at eight at night.
drills.hint: the period word for the hours of darkness

points.title: Politeness formulas: asante, tafadhali, samahani, pole, karibu
points.function: Thank, request, apologise, sympathise and welcome using the fixed courtesy words.
points.explanation: Five short words carry most everyday courtesy, and each has a distinct job. Asante thanks, strengthened as asante sana and pluralised as asanteni. Tafadhali marks a request as polite and may open or close it. Samahani apologises for something you did, or opens a request to a stranger. Pole is not an apology at all: it expresses sympathy for somebody else's misfortune, which is why pole sana is said to someone who is ill or has suffered a loss. Karibu welcomes, with karibuni for several people, and doubles as the reply to asante. Confusing samahani with pole is the commonest learner error.

drills.translation: Thank you very much for your help.
drills.hint: the word of gratitude, singular addressee

drills.translation: Thank you all for coming today.
drills.hint: the word of gratitude with the plural addressee suffix

drills.translation: Please close the door.
drills.hint: the word that softens a command into a request

drills.translation: Bring me water, please.
drills.hint: the word that softens a command into a request

drills.translation: Sorry, I am late.
drills.hint: the apology used when you are at fault

drills.translation: Excuse me, which is the way to the station?
drills.hint: the apology word used to open a question to a stranger

drills.translation: I am so sorry about your illness.
drills.hint: the word offering sympathy for another's misfortune

drills.translation: You fell? Oh dear!
drills.hint: the word offering sympathy for another's misfortune

drills.translation: Welcome to our home.
Welcome, all guests.
drills.hint: the welcoming word with the plural addressee suffix

drills.translation: Thanks for the food. You're welcome.
drills.hint: the standard reply to thanks, identical to the welcoming word

drills.translation: I have stepped on your foot, sorry.
drills.hint: the apology used when you are at fault

points.title: Talking about illness: ninaumwa na and inaniuma
points.function: Say which part of the body hurts, using either the passive or the active construction.
points.explanation: Swahili has two standard ways of reporting pain, and both differ from English. The first makes the sufferer the subject of a passive verb and names the body part as the agent: ninaumwa na kichwa, literally 'I am hurt by the head', meaning 'I have a headache'. The second makes the body part the subject of the active verb and puts the sufferer in as an object infix: kichwa kinaniuma, 'the head hurts me'. The infix must agree with the person and the subject prefix with the body part's class, so mgongo unaniuma but macho yananiuma. For a general statement of being unwell, mimi ni mgonjwa or sijisikii vizuri are the usual phrases.

drills.translation: I have had a headache since morning.
drills.hint: the class 7 body part that sits on the shoulders

drills.translation: His leg hurts after running.
drills.hint: the class 3 body part you walk on

drills.translation: My back hurts me when I sit a long time.
drills.hint: class 3 subject, first person object, present tense of the hurt verb

drills.sentence: Macho yake {{answer}} kwa sababu ya vumbi.
drills.translation: Her eyes hurt her because of the dust.
drills.hint: class 6 subject, class 1 object, present tense of the hurt verb
drills.gloss: macho (CL6-eye) y-ake (CL6-her) ___ kwa sababu ya (because.of) vumbi (CL5-dust)

drills.translation: My child is ill today.
drills.hint: the class 1 noun for somebody who is ill

drills.translation: I have not been feeling well since yesterday.
drills.hint: first person negative reflexive of the verb meaning to feel

drills.translation: The doctor asked, what is hurting you?
drills.hint: the interrogative asking about a thing

drills.translation: My stomach has hurt since I ate the fish.
drills.hint: class 5 subject, first person object, present tense of the hurt verb

prerequisites: States expressed with nina: njaa, kiu, wasiwasi, huzuni

points.title: Ordinal numbers: wa kwanza, ya pili, cha tatu
points.function: Say first, second, third and so on, with the linker agreeing with the noun's class.
points.explanation: Ordinals are built from the cardinal numbers with the -a of association in front, and that linker carries the noun's class concord: mtu wa kwanza, siku ya pili, kitabu cha tatu, gari la nne. Only 'first' has its own word, kwanza, which is not the cardinal moja; from two upwards the cardinal is simply reused — pili, tatu, nne. Note that pili is used for 'second' rather than mbili. The ordinal always follows its noun. The same linker appears in dates and floors: ghorofa ya tatu, mwezi wa kumi.

drills.translation: He is the first child.
The second guest has arrived.
On the third day we travelled to Mombasa.
Our room is on the fourth floor.
The second book is harder.
The first session was long.
The third car is mine.
The first lesson starts at eight.
The first month is January.
drills.hint: the special word for the ordinal one, not the cardinal

drills.sentence: Hii ni mara ya {{answer}} kutembelea Kenya.
drills.translation: This is the second time visiting Kenya.
drills.hint: the ordinal for two, which differs from the cardinal mbili
drills.gloss: hii (CL9-this) ni (is) mara (CL9-time) ya (CL9-of) ___ ku-tembelea (INF-visit) Kenya

prerequisites: Numbers 11 to 100, and talking about prices

points.title: Impersonal verbs: inabidi, inafaa, inawezekana
points.function: Express obligation, suitability and possibility with a verb that has no real subject.
points.explanation: A small group of verbs takes the class 9 prefix i- as a dummy subject, standing for the situation as a whole rather than any person. Inabidi expresses obligation, inafaa suitability or advisability, and inawezekana possibility. The person affected is carried as an object infix on the impersonal verb, and the following verb goes into the subjunctive: inanibidi niende, 'it obliges me that I go', meaning 'I have to go'. This differs from lazima, which is a noun and simply precedes a subjunctive without any infix. The negative uses ha-: haifai, haiwezekani.

drills.translation: I have to go to hospital today.
drills.hint: impersonal present with a first person object infix, from the oblige verb

drills.translation: They have to come back tomorrow morning.
drills.hint: impersonal present with a class 2 object infix, from the oblige verb

drills.translation: It is advisable that we arrive early tomorrow.
drills.hint: impersonal present of the verb meaning to be suitable

drills.sentence: {{answer}} kunywa maji mengi wakati wa joto.
drills.translation: It is advisable to drink plenty of water in hot weather.
drills.hint: impersonal present of the verb meaning to be suitable
drills.gloss: ___ ku-nywa (INF-drink) maji (CL6-water) m-engi (CL6-much) wakati (CL11-time) wa (CL11-of) joto (CL5-heat)

drills.translation: It is possible that it may rain in the evening.
drills.hint: impersonal present of the verb meaning to be possible

drills.translation: Is it possible to get there by bus?
drills.hint: impersonal present of the verb meaning to be possible

drills.translation: It is not appropriate to smoke here.
drills.hint: impersonal negative of the verb meaning to be suitable

drills.translation: You must go right now.
drills.hint: the noun meaning necessity, used before a subjunctive

drills.translation: I had to leave work early yesterday.
drills.hint: first person subjunctive of the verb meaning to depart

drills.sentence: {{answer}} kuahirisha safari kwa sababu ya dhoruba.
drills.translation: It was necessary to postpone the journey because of the storm.
drills.hint: impersonal past of the oblige verb, with no object infix
drills.gloss: ___ ku-ahirisha (INF-postpone) safari (CL9-journey) kwa sababu ya (because.of) dhoruba (CL9-storm)

prerequisites: States expressed with nina: njaa, kiu, wasiwasi, huzuni

points.title: Dates, months and birthdays
points.function: Give a date, name a month, and say when a birthday falls.
points.explanation: Month names are borrowed and unchanged: Januari, Februari, Machi, Aprili, Mei, Juni, Julai, Agosti, Septemba, Oktoba, Novemba, Desemba. A date is built with tarehe, 'date', followed by the plain cardinal number and then the month: tarehe nne Aprili. The number takes no concord here. Months can also be counted rather than named — mwezi wa nne, 'the fourth month', is a common alternative to Aprili. A birthday is siku ya kuzaliwa, literally 'the day of being born', and the question is siku yako ya kuzaliwa ni lini?

drills.translation: I was born on the thirteenth of June.
The meeting is on the first of December.
The holiday begins in December.
drills.hint: the last month of the year

drills.translation: School opens in January.
drills.hint: the first month of the year

drills.translation: I will travel in the fourth month.
He arrived in the eighth month.
When is your birthday?
drills.hint: the passive infinitive meaning to come into the world

drills.translation: We will celebrate her birthday on Saturday.
drills.hint: the passive infinitive meaning to come into the world

drills.translation: She was born on the twenty-second of August.
drills.hint: the numeral for a pair, with no concord after tarehe

drills.sentence: Mwezi wa kwanza wa mwaka ni {{answer}}.
drills.translation: The first month of the year is January.
drills.hint: the month that opens the calendar
drills.gloss: mwezi (CL3-month) wa (CL3-of) kwanza (first) wa (CL3-of) mwaka (CL3-year) ni (is) ___

points.title: States expressed with nina: njaa, kiu, wasiwasi, huzuni
points.function: Say how you feel using the have-construction, where English uses the verb to be.
points.explanation: Swahili expresses many bodily and emotional states as things you possess rather than things you are. Nina njaa is literally 'I have hunger' and means 'I am hungry'; nina kiu means 'I am thirsty'; nina baridi, 'I have cold', means 'I feel cold'. The same pattern covers wasiwasi (worry), huzuni (sadness) and homa (fever). The construction is the subject prefix plus -na, so it inflects normally: una njaa?, ana homa, tuna kiu. The negative uses the negative subject prefix: sina njaa. Note the contrast with kuna baridi, which describes the weather rather than the person.

drills.translation: I am hungry; let's go and eat.
drills.hint: first person singular of the have-construction

drills.translation: The child has had a fever since yesterday.
Are you thirsty? Shall I bring you water?
drills.hint: second person singular of the have-construction

drills.translation: Are you worried about the journey?
drills.hint: second person singular of the have-construction

drills.translation: I am not hungry; I have already eaten.
drills.hint: first person singular negative of the have-construction

drills.translation: I am not sad, only tired.
drills.hint: first person singular negative of the have-construction

drills.translation: It is cold outside today.
drills.hint: the class 17 existential meaning there is

drills.translation: There is fierce heat this afternoon.
drills.hint: the class 17 existential meaning there is

drills.sentence: Baada ya kutembea mbali, tulikuwa na {{answer}} sana.
drills.translation: After walking far, we were very thirsty.
drills.hint: the state noun meaning a need to drink
drills.gloss: baada ya (after) ku-tembea (INF-walk) mbali (far) tu-li-kuwa na (1PL-PAST-be with) ___ sana (very)

drills.translation: She is sad because she has lost her job.
